item.title: Google Bigquery Counting Element Frequency In Bigquery Array Field A How To Guide
item.description: Objective: Count frequency of elements in a BigQuery array field Table structure: The table has four columns - author_id, year, and three columns l_0, l_1, and l_2, that contain an array of strings. Desired output: A table that gives a frequency count of the elements in the fields l_0, l_1, and l_2. Assumptions: The desired output is on a per-array basis. Solution: One way to achieve the desired output is to use the UNNEST function to flatten the array fields and then count the frequency of each element. We can then use the ANY_VALUE function to group the remaining columns. The following query demonstrates this approach: SELECT author_id, year, (SELECT ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(name, count)) FROM ( SELECT l_0 AS name, COUNT(*) AS count FROM UNNEST(l_0) AS l_0 GROUP BY 1 ) ) AS l_0, (SELECT ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(name, count)) FROM ( SELECT l_1 AS name, COUNT(*) AS count FROM UNNEST(l_1) AS l_1 GROUP BY 1 ) ) AS l_1, (SELECT ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(name, count)) FROM ( SELECT l_2 AS name, COUNT(*) AS count FROM UNNEST(l_2) AS l_2 GROUP BY 1 ) ) AS l_2 FROM my_table GROUP BY author_id, year Let’s break down the code line by line: - The first part of the query is the column selection for author_id and year. SELECT author_id, year, - We then determine the frequency of elements in the l_0 array using the UNNEST function to flatten it and counting the frequency of each element using the COUNT function. We can then use ARRAY_AGG function to collect the counts and names into an array of structs. (SELECT ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(name, count)) FROM ( SELECT l_0 AS name, COUNT(*) AS count FROM UNNEST(l_0) AS l_0 GROUP BY 1 ) ) AS l_0, - The same approach is repeated for the l_1 and l_2 arrays. (SELECT ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(name, count)) FROM ( SELECT l_1 AS name, COUNT(*) AS count FROM UNNEST(l_1) AS l_1 GROUP BY 1 ) ) AS l_1, (SELECT ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(name, count)) FROM ( SELECT l_2 AS name, COUNT(*) AS count FROM UNNEST(l_2) AS l_2 GROUP BY 1 ) ) AS l_2 - Lastly, we group our results by author_id and year. FROM my_table GROUP BY author_id, year Alternative ways: Another approach to count the frequency of elements in a BigQuery array field is to use the STRUCT and UNNEST functions to flatten the array and then aggregate the results using GROUP BY. Here is an example: ``` SELECT author_id, year, ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(l_0.name AS name, l_0.count AS count)) AS l_0, ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(l_1.name AS name, l_1.count AS count)) AS l_1, ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(l_2.name AS name, l_2.count AS count)) AS l_2 FROM ( SELECT author_id, year, name, COUNT(*) AS count FROM my_table, UNNEST(l_0) AS name GROUP BY author_id, year, name ) l_0 FULL OUTER JOIN ( SELECT]]>

Creating Partitioned Table in BigQuery through CLI

To create a partitioned table using the CLI, run the following command:

bq query --use_legacy_sql=false '
CREATE TABLE [DATASET].[TABLENAME] (
    [COLUMN] [DATATYPE],
    ...
    [COLUMN] [DATATYPE],
    [PARTITION_COLUMN] DATE)
PARTITION BY [PARTITION_COLUMN]
OPTIONS(
  expiration_timestamp=TIMESTAMP "2028-01-01 00:00:00 UTC",
  description="Example partitioned table create in BQ CLI",
  labels=[("partition","summary")]
);'

The command above creates a table with the given table name and dataset name in BigQuery. The table schema contains one or more columns defined by column_name and data_type.
The partition column is defined by the column name on which you want to partition the table. Here, the date column is chosen for partitioning.
The OPTIONS parameter sets the expiration date for the table, adds description, and sets labels.

item.description:
Querying tables in BigQuery: Wildcard vs Time Partitioned Tables

Introduction

When it comes to querying tables in BigQuery, there are different approaches that can be taken. Two of the most common ones are the use of Wildcard Tables and Time Partitioned Tables. In this post, we will explore the differences between these approaches and their implications.

What is a Wildcard Table?

item.title: Google Bigquery Differentiating Totalbytesbilled Totalbytesprocessed
item.description:
Learning totalBytesBilled and totalBytesProcessed in BigQuery

What are totalBytesBilled and totalBytesProcessed?

totalBytesBilled and totalBytesProcessed are statistics provided by Google BigQuery that track the amount of data processed and billed for a particular query or job. Here, “processed” refers to the amount of data that was actually read and used by the query, while “billed” refers to the amount of data that was reserved in advance to execute the query.

What is the difference between totalBytesBilled and totalBytesProcessed?

totalBytesProcessed refers to the amount of data read and processed by BigQuery to execute the query. This includes data that was read from storage, as well as any intermediate data created during the query execution. totalBytesBilled, on the other hand, refers to the amount of data reserved by BigQuery for the query in advance. This includes data that may have been filtered out before it was processed, as well as any data that was read but ultimately not used in the query. As a result, it is possible for totalBytesBilled to be higher than totalBytesProcessed, particularly for small queries that are run on heavily constrained systems where BigQuery needs to reserve resources in advance to ensure that the query completes quickly.

item.description:
How to extract date from timestamp in Bigquery using standardSQL?
In Bigquery, timestamps can be extracted using standardSQL. There are two methods available for extracting dates from a timestamp in Bigquery:

#1. Using DATE() and TIMESTAMP_MILLIS() functions

The first method involves using the DATE() and TIMESTAMP_MILLIS() functions. Here’s how:

# standardSQL query
SELECT DATE(TIMESTAMP_MILLIS(CAST((timestamp) AS INT64))) AS date
FROM YourTable;

In the above query:

  • The TIMESTAMP_MILLIS() function is used to convert timestamp to milliseconds.
  • The CAST() function is used to cast the timestamp value as INT64.
  • The DATE() function is used to extract the date from the timestamp value in milliseconds.

item.description:

Summary

While running a streaming Apache Beam pipeline in Google Dataflow, which reads data from Kafka and streams inserts to Bigquery, a large number of warnings were thrown during the Bigquery streaming insert step. The error message reads “java.lang.RuntimeException: ManagedChannel allocation site”.

Explanation

The error message suggests that the issue is related to the gRPC channel provided by Google’s API Gateway. These errors occur when there is an issue with the creation or allocation of channels in gRPC, which could happen due to various reasons including network connectivity issues or resource constraints. In this specific case, the issue could be related to the fact that the pipeline is attempting to insert data into Bigquery at a higher rate than the channel can handle. It is also possible that the Dataflow VMs running the pipeline may have reached their network bandwidth limits. The error message suggests that the issue is related to the creation of the ManagedChannel, which is established by the InstantiatingGrpcChannelProvider. When creating a Bigquery client, the method first creates a ChannelPool and then a channel for every stream. In this process, if any of the channels created fail, the error message may occur.

item.title: Google Bigquery Executing One Query At A Time With Bigquery
item.description:
BigQuery executing only one query

Summary:

In BigQuery, while running a query in the UI, if you get the error “Error: 6.1 - 0.0: Only one query can be executed at a time,” it means that the query string has been parsed as containing multiple queries. This error occurs when there are multiple top-level SELECT statements in the query text box.

Explanation:

When running a query in BigQuery, you can only execute one query at a time. This means that you cannot have multiple top-level SELECT statements in the query text box. The error message “Error: 6.1 - 0.0: Only one query can be executed at a time” indicates that the query string has been parsed as containing multiple queries. The second query may be beginning on or around line 6. To fix this error, check the query text box to ensure that there are no multiple top-level SELECT statements. If there are, remove them or split them into separate queries.

Using SPLIT() Function

If you want to find the most common bi-grams using the SPLIT() function, you can use the following code:

SELECT word, nextword, COUNT(*) c 
FROM (
SELECT pos, title, word, LEAD(word) OVER(PARTITION BY created_utc,title ORDER BY pos) nextword FROM (
SELECT created_utc, title, word, pos FROM FLATTEN(
  (SELECT created_utc, title, SPLIT(title, ' ') word FROM [bigquery-samples:reddit.full])
  ), word)
))
WHERE nextword IS NOT null
GROUP EACH BY 1, 2
ORDER BY c DESC
LIMIT 100

item.description:
Invalid JSON Formatting Error
When attempting to import this JSON into a Google BigQuery table, the following error appeared:

JSON table encountered too many errors, giving up. Rows: 1; errors: 1. (error code: invalid)

JSON parsing error in row starting at position 0 at file: file-00000000. Start of array encountered without start of object. (error code: invalid)

More, jsonformatter.org also reports a parsing error for this JSON block.

The Invalid JSON

[{'instrument_token': 11192834, 'average_price': 8463.45, 'last_price': 8471.1, 'last_quantity': 75, 'buy_quantity': 1065150, 'volume': 5545950, 'depth': {'buy': [{'price': 8471.1, 'quantity': 300, 'orders': 131072}, {'price': 8471.0, 'quantity': 300, 'orders': 65536}, {'price': 8470.95, 'quantity': 150, 'orders': 65536}, {'price': 8470.85, 'quantity': 75, 'orders': 65536}, {'price': 8470.7, 'quantity': 225, 'orders': 65536}], 'sell': [{'price': 8471.5, 'quantity': 150, 'orders': 131072}, {'price': 8471.55, 'quantity': 375, 'orders': 327680}, {'price': 8471.8, 'quantity': 1050, 'orders': 65536}, {'price': 8472.0, 'quantity': 1050, 'orders': 327680}, {'price': 8472.1, 'quantity': 150, 'orders': 65536}]}, 'ohlc': {'high': 8484.1, 'close': 8336.45, 'low': 8422.35, 'open': 8432.75}, 'mode': 'quote', 'sell_quantity': 998475, 'tradeable': True, 'change': 1.6151959167271395}]

item.title: Google Bigquery Fixing Not A Leaf Field Error In Bigquery
item.description:
How to Fix the “Not a Leaf Field” Error in BigQuery If you are trying to run a query in BigQuery and getting the “Not a Leaf Field” error, you are not alone. This error occurs when you try to select a nested field that is not a leaf field. Here’s how to fix it.

Learning the Error

The error “Field payload.pages from table publicdata:samples.github_nested is not a leaf field” means that the field you are trying to select is a nested field and not a leaf field. A leaf field is a field that does not contain any other fields. In contrast, a nested field is a field that contains one or more fields. In BigQuery, you can only select leaf fields, so you need to flatten the nested field before you can select it.

Currently, there are three possible values: US, EU, and unspecified. If you specify US, your data is stored in us-central1 and us-central2. If you specify EU, your data is stored in europe-west1. item.description:

If you want to get the first record of a specific column in BigQuery, you can use the hits.time column which represents the number of milliseconds after the visitStartTime when the hit was recorded. The first hit has a hits.time of 0, so you just have to query for hits.time=0.

Example:

SELECT 
  STRFTIME_UTC_USEC(date, '%U') AS WK, 
  visitId, 
  date AS SALES_DATE, 
  hits.eventInfo.eventLabel AS SEARCH_DD, 
  year(date) as yr, 
  hits.time AS t
FROM
  (TABLE_DATE_RANGE([67977396.ga_sessions_], TIMESTAMP('2015-03-04'), TIMESTAMP('2015-03-04')))
WHERE 
  hits.eventInfo.eventAction='Depart date' 
  AND hits.eventInfo.eventCategory='Book a train'
  AND hits.time=0
ORDER BY 
  visitId

The query above selects the first record of the hits.time column for each visitId. It retrieves the week number, visitId, date, eventLabel, year and hits.time column. The results are filtered by the specified conditions, and ordered by visitId.

item.title: Google Bigquery How To Get Table Schema Using Python Bigquery Api
item.description:
Python BigQuery API - Get Table Schema BigQuery is a cloud-based data warehouse and storage solution provided by Google. In this post, we will be discussing how to fetch the schema of a table using the Python BigQuery API.

Dependencies

Before we begin, you need to install the following dependencies:

  • google-cloud-bigquery library
  • google-cloud-storage library

Code Explanation

The below code fetches the schema of a table in BigQuery:

from google.cloud import bigquery
from google.cloud import storage

# Creating BigQuery client object
client =  bigquery.Client.from_service_account_json('service_account.json')

def extract_table_schema(client): 
    # Setting up BigQuery dataset and table id
    project = "bigquery-public-data"
    dataset_id = 'samples'
    table_id = 'shakespeare'

    # Constructing BigQuery reference objects
    dataset_ref = client.dataset(dataset_id, project=project)
    table_ref = dataset_ref.table(table_id)
    
    # Fetching Table metadata
    table = client.get_table(table_ref) 

    # Parsing Table Schema
    schema = table.schema
    schema_list = []

    for field in schema:
        schema_list.append(field.name + ' ' + field.field_type)

    # Returning schema as string
    return ','.join(schema_list)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    table_schema = extract_table_schema(client)
    print(table_schema)

Code Breakdown

  • First, we import the necessary libraries - google.cloud.bigquery and google.cloud.storage
  • A BigQuery client object is created using the service account credentials stored in service_account.json
  • We define a function extract_table_schema that takes the BigQuery client object as input
  • Next, we define the project id, the dataset id, and the table id that we want to fetch schema from
  • We create BigQuery dataset and table reference objects using the client object and ids defined above
  • The get_table method of the client object is used to fetch metadata about the table
  • The schema of the table is accessed using the schema property of the table object
  • We iterate over the fields in the schema and add a string with the format fieldname fieldtype to a list
  • Lastly, the list is joined using commas and returned as a string

Code Output

The function returns the schema of the specified table as a comma-separated string with each field in the format fieldname fieldtype

item.title: Google Bigquery Limit Array Elements In Bigquery Table Get First N
item.description:
How to get the first N elements from an array column in a BigQuery table without unnesting, ranking, and aggregating back to an array?

Solution A general solution with a User-Defined Function (UDF) that can be called for any array type is as follows:

CREATE TEMP FUNCTION TopN(arr ANY TYPE, n INT64) AS (
  ARRAY(SELECT x FROM UNNEST(arr) AS x WITH OFFSET off WHERE off < n ORDER BY off)
);

WITH data AS
(
  SELECT 1001 as id, ['a', 'b', 'c'] as array_1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 1002 as id, ['d', 'e', 'f', 'g'] as array_1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 1003 as id, ['h', 'i'] as array_1
)
SELECT *, TopN(array_1, 2) AS my_result
FROM data

The above code first defines a UDF called TopN that takes two inputs - an array and a number, and returns the first N elements of the array while keeping the array data type. The UDF uses UNNEST to convert the input array into a table and adds an offset to each element. It then selects the elements that have an offset less than N and orders them by offset to preserve their original order in the array. Lastly, the UDF returns an array that consists of the selected elements.

item.title: Google Bigquery Mastering Big Querys Distinct On Group By Functions
item.description:
Selecting the First Row in Each Group Using BigQuery

Summary

The aim is to select the first comment, in terms of created_utc, for each link_id (Reddit submission). It can be achieved by using GROUP BY along with ROW_NUMBER() and PARTITION BY clauses.

Dataset

The dataset used in this example is fh-bigquery:reddit_comments.2018_01.

Code Explanation

To retrieve the first comment related to each link_id, we can use the following query:

SELECT 
  ARRAY_AGG(body ORDER BY created_utc LIMIT 1)[OFFSET(0)] body, 
  link_id
FROM `fh-bigquery.reddit_comments.2018_01`
WHERE subreddit_id = 't5_2zkvo'
GROUP BY link_id

Here, we are using ARRAY_AGG() function that returns an array of values of a specified expression. We use body and link_id as expressions here. The LIMIT 1 argument fetches only the first row for each link_id based on its created_utc value. The OFFSET(0) argument extracts the element from the array. Lastly, we use the GROUP BY statement to group the results by link_id.

SELECT NTH(2,SPLIT('FIRST-SECOND','-')) as second_part FROM [FOO.bar] limit 10

Learning SHA256 Hashing

SHA256 (Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit) is a cryptographic hash function used to convert data of any size into a fixed size output. The output of a hash function is a unique, fixed-length string that represents the original input data. The hash function is designed to be a one-way function and provides a high level of security for data integrity.

item.title: Google Bigquery Preserving Integer Data Type In Json Export A Guide
item.description:
How to Preserve Integer Data Type when Exporting BigQuery Tables to JSON
When exporting BigQuery tables in JSON format, the INTEGER fields are converted to strings. This can be problematic for data analysis purposes since the data type is important for certain operations. This post aims to explain why this happens and provide alternative solutions to preserve integer data types.

Why are INTEGER fields converted to strings in JSON format?

The reason for this phenomenon is due to a combination of the Javascript specification, IEEE floating point precision, JSON, and BigQuery integer sizes. In Javascript, all numbers must be representable as IEEE754 double-precision floating point values. When parsing JSON numbers, Javascript numbers are used, which cannot always represent all 64-bit integer values used in BigQuery tables (which uses 64-bit signed integer values).

item.title: Google Bigquery Prevent Duplicates In Bigquery
item.description:

At times, you may encounter a situation where you would want to avoid inserting duplicates into a Bigquery table. Unfortunately, there is no primary key or unique constraint support on Bigquery. Although, there are still several ways to avoid duplicates.

The Append-only Model of Bigquery

In Bigquery, everything is append-only. That means that for any new update, a new row is added. This design choice allows us to leverage insights from every new update we add to the same row. For example, we might want to track how long it takes for the end-user to choose their country during signup flow. Since we have a dropdown of countries, it will take some time until it scrolls to their country. By appending rows for each snapshot, we can calculate the time it takes to make the selection. Moreover, we can identify how we can optimize this process using data.

Summary:

This Q&A Session explains how to query a BYTES field in Google BigQuery using SQL. It also provides solutions to some common errors while querying the BYTES field in BigQuery.

Querying BYTES Field in BigQuery:

BYTES is a binary data type used to store data in a byte array format. In Google BigQuery, we can use SQL to query tables that include BYTES field. To query a BYTES field, we need to use the FROM_BASE64() function to convert the Base64-encoded string to BYTES format. Here’s an example query: sql SELECT * FROM `project\_name.dataset\_name.table\_name` WHERE field_name = FROM_BASE64('16D6M7PN3w7Cn8mJyrmrUSZY9ummMf5QCGEMuiSmSlw='); In the query above, ‘16D6M7PN3w7Cn8mJyrmrUSZY9ummMf5QCGEMuiSmSlw=’ is the Base64 encoded string that we want to match with the BYTES field. More, we can also use a bytes literal that starts with ‘b’ to match the BYTES field. Here’s an updated query: sql SELECT * FROM `project\_name.dataset\_name.table\_name` WHERE field_name = b'16D6M7PN3w7Cn8mJyrmrUSZY9ummMf5QCGEMuiSmSlw='; In the query above, we are using the bytes literal ‘b’ followed by the Base64 encoded string to match the BYTES field.

item.title: Google Bigquery Querying Bigquery Table With Write_Truncate Is It Safe
item.description:
Can I safely query a BigQuery table being replaced with WRITE_TRUNCATE?

Introduction:

When a BigQuery load job is performed and the writeDisposition parameter is set to WRITE_TRUNCATE, it replaces the contents of the target table with the loaded data. During this process, users may wonder if they can query the table safely without any errors.

Answer:

Yes, it is safe to query a BigQuery table being replaced with WRITE_TRUNCATE during a load job. The WRITE_TRUNCATE is an atomic operation that gets applied at the end of the load job. Therefore, any queries that happen during that time will see either only the old data or all of the new data. There should be no cases where an error occurs while querying the table.

item.title: Google Bigquery Querying Dates In Bigquery 3 Days Prior Earlier

Querying BigQuery Where Date is Less Than or Equal to 3 Days Minus Current Date In this post, we will discuss how to create a query in BigQuery to only return data where the date is minus 3 days from the current date. We will walk through each line of the code and provide explanations.

Query Syntax:

#standardSQL
WITH yourTable AS (
  SELECT i, date
  FROM UNNEST(GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY('2017-04-15', '2017-04-28')) AS date WITH OFFSET AS i
)
SELECT *
FROM yourTable
WHERE date <= DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 3 DAY)

Explanation:

The query uses Standard SQL syntax in BigQuery. We start with a “WITH” clause that defines a common table expression (CTE) named “yourTable.” This CTE generates an array of dates between ‘2017-04-15’ and ‘2017-04-28’ using the GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY function. The dates are then assigned an index value using the OFFSET function.

item.title: Google Bigquery Round Timestamp To Nearest 15 Minute Intervals In Bigquery
item.description:
Question: How can I round a timestamp to the nearest 15-minute interval using BigQuery standard SQL?

Solution:

To round a timestamp to the nearest 15-minute interval in BigQuery standard SQL, you can use the following formula:

TIMESTAMP_SECONDS(900 * DIV(UNIX_SECONDS(dt_from) + 450, 900))

This formula works by converting the timestamp to Unix time (the number of seconds since January 1, 1970), adding 450 seconds (7.5 minutes) to it, dividing the result by 900 (the number of seconds in 15 minutes), rounding down to the nearest integer, and then multiplying by 900 to get the Unix time of the nearest 15-minute interval. Lastly, the Unix time is converted back to a timestamp using the TIMESTAMP_SECONDS function.

item.title: Google Bigquery Selecting Table_Id In Bigquery Table Wildcard Query
item.description:
Bigquery Table Wildcard Query using _TABLE_SUFFIX Pseudocolumn
Table Wildcard Query is used in BigQuery to query data from multiple tables with similar schema using wildcard characters. BigQuery provides the _TABLE_SUFFIX pseudocolumn that allows users to dynamically reference the table_id.

Code Explanation

The following code demonstrates the use of _TABLE_SUFFIX pseudocolumn to select all available data and group it by the column of interest and the day it was captured.

SELECT _TABLE_SUFFIX as table_id, 
       identifier, 
       Sum(AppAnalytic) as AppAnalyticCount 
FROM `database_main.Title_*` 
WHERE length(_TABLE_SUFFIX) >= 4 
GROUP BY identifier, table_id 
ORDER BY AppAnalyticCount DESC 
LIMIT 10
  • The first line of the code uses the SELECT clause to select _TABLE_SUFFIX pseudocolumn and aliases it as table_id.
  • The second line of the code selects the identifier column.
  • The third line of the code computes the sum of the AppAnalytic column and aliases it as AppAnalyticCount.
  • The fourth line of code uses the FROM clause to specify the dataset and the tables to query using wildcards. In this example, all tables with the prefix Title_ is queried.
  • The WHERE statement filters the tables that have a length greater than or equal to 4.
  • The GROUP BY clause groups the data by the identifier, and table_id columns, allowing us to analyze the data based on the day or time period.
  • The ORDER BY clause orders the data based on� AppAnalyticCount column in descending order.
  • The LIMIT clause limits the number of results returned to the top 10.

Practical Example

An example use case of this query is analyzing website traffic by capturing data on a day-sharded basis. BigQuery tables are created in a daily basis, and the rows contain time-stamped and non-time-stamped data. We can use table wildcard to retrieve data from specific tables and analyze each table to determine the web page that generated the most amount of traffic on a particular day based on their identifier.

item.title: Google Bigquery Slow Apache Beam Bigqueryio Write Time
item.description:
Problem The Apache Beam pipeline is writing to an unpartitioned BigQuery target table with millions of TableRows in the PCollection. BigQueryIO is creating a temp file for every single record in the BigQueryWriteTemp temp folder, leading to poor performance when running with DirectRunner. Is this behavior expected?

Solution

Yes, the behavior is expected. BigQueryIO writes TableRow objects in parallel by using a temporary file per output partition. Since the target table is unpartitioned, each TableRow will be written to its own temporary file. This can lead to an overwhelming number of temp files and poor performance when running with a DirectRunner.

What can I expect from BigQuery’s performance with small datasets?

item.title: Google Bigquery Stripping Non Numeric Characters From Bigquery Results
item.description:
How to Convert Dollar Amounts to Numbers in BigQuery

Problem

You have dollar amounts in your BigQuery results that you want to convert into pure numbers, but you don’t know how to do it using BigQuery functions.

Solution

You can use regular expressions to remove non-numeric characters from the dollar amounts and then cast the resulting string to an integer. Here’s an example query:

#standardSQL
WITH `project.dataset.table` AS (
  SELECT '$15,000' AS dollar_amount UNION ALL
  SELECT '$25,000' UNION ALL
  SELECT '$10,000' 
)
SELECT 
  dollar_amount, 
  CAST(REGEXP_REPLACE(dollar_amount, r'$|,', '') as INT64) amount
FROM `project.dataset.table`

The query selects the dollar amounts from the sample table project.dataset.table. It then uses the REGEXP_REPLACE function to remove the $ and , characters from each dollar amount using a regular expression. Lastly, it casts the resulting string to an INT64 using the CAST function.

In BigQuery, FIRST_VALUE is an analytic function that can be used to return the first value in a list, while IGNORE_NULLS is an optional parameter that can be included to ignore any null values in the list.

Let’s consider the following example:

WITH finishers AS (SELECT 'Bob' as name, TIMESTAMP '2016-10-18 2:51:45' as finish_time, 'F30-34' as division UNION ALL SELECT NULL, TIMESTAMP '2016-10-18 2:54:11', 'F35-39' UNION ALL SELECT 'Mary', TIMESTAMP '2016-10-18 2:59:01', 'F35-39' UNION ALL SELECT 'John', TIMESTAMP '2016-10-18 3:01:17', 'F35-39'
)
SELECT *, FIRST_VALUE(name IGNORE NULLS) OVER(PARTITION BY division ORDER BY finish_time) AS fastest_in_division
FROM finishers
ORDER by division

This query selects data from a CTE called finishers, which contains details of a running race, including the name of each participant, the time they finished the race, and the division they competed in. The query then uses the FIRST_VALUE and IGNORE_NULLS functions to return the fastest participant in each division.

item.title: Google Bigquery Unexpected Entity Type
item.description:
Entity was of unexpected kind error when loading Firestore exports to BigQuery

Problem

When loading Firestore exports to BigQuery, you may encounter an error that says “Entity was of unexpected kind”.

Solution

  • Ensure that documents in the export data share a consistent schema. This means that each document in the collection should have the same fields with the same data types.
  • Make sure that you specify a collection-ids filter in your export command. Data exported without specifying a collection ID filter cannot be loaded into BigQuery.
  • Load data from Firestore, not from Datastore. Follow the steps given in this link to load your Firestore data to BigQuery.

Explanation

Firestore is a NoSQL document database, which means that each document in a collection can have a different structure. Although, when loading the data into BigQuery, each row in the table must have the same schema. If documents in your Firestore export data have different structures, you will encounter the “Entity was of unexpected kind” error. Another possible reason for this error is that you did not specify a collection-ids filter when exporting the data from Firestore. When exporting data, you can specify a collection-ids filter to only export data from specific collections. If you did not specify a filter and exported all data, BigQuery will not be able to determine which collection a row belongs to, resulting in the “Entity was of unexpected kind” error. Lastly, make sure that you follow the correct steps to load Firestore data to BigQuery. Loading Datastore exports to BigQuery is a different process and may not work with Firestore data.

item.title: Google Bigquery Unnesting Structs In Bigquery
item.description:
Flattening Structs with Multiple Arrays in BigQuery

Summary:

In BigQuery, if you have a struct with multiple arrays that you want to flatten to perform analysis, you can use the UNNEST operator to do so. The UNNEST operator works by converting the array into a table where each row represents an element in the original array.

Code Explanation:

sql SELECT origin, s.destination, s.visitors FROM dataset.table t CROSS JOIN UNNEST(t.struct) AS s; The code above selects data from a table called table in the dataset dataset. It then uses the CROSS JOIN command on the UNNEST operator to convert the struct column in the table into a table of elements. The UNNEST function is used twice since there are two arrays we want to flatten, destination and visitors. The AS s creates a named alias for the flattened table. s represents the flattened struct element. The columns of the flattened table can now be accessed using the alias. We can query the newly flattened table by specifying the columns we want to keep (in this case, origin, destination, and visitors). This query essentially generates a Cartesian product, where each destination is paired with every row in the visitors array.

item.title: Google Bigquery Use Cosine Similarity In Bigquery Sql
item.description:
Computing Cosine Similarity with BigQuery SQL If you have vectors stored in BigQuery and want to find the most similar between them, you can use BigQuery standard SQL to compute the cosine similarity. The following query looks at the vector defined for each document, given its dimensions (by word) and multiplies them with the cosine distance formula:

SELECT ANY_VALUE(title2) orig, ANY_VALUE(tf2id) id_orig, a.id id_similar 
  , ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE( SUM(b.tf_idf * IFNULL(c.tf_idf,0)),(SQRT(SUM(b.tf_idf*b.tf_idf))*SQRT(SUM(POW(IFNULL(c.tf_idf,0),2))))),4) distance
  , ANY_VALUE(title1) similar
  , ARRAY_AGG((ROUND(b.tf_idf,4), ROUND(c.tf_idf,4))) weights
  , ARRAY_AGG((b.word, c.word)) words
FROM (
  SELECT id, tfidfs tf1, tf2, tf2id
  , a.title title1
  , b.title title2
  FROM `your_table_name` a
  CROSS JOIN (
    SELECT tfidfs tf2, id tf2id, title 
    FROM `your_table_name`
    WHERE id = 11353679 
    LIMIT 1
  ) b
) a

item.description:

Summary

In MySQL, Oracle and Teradata, the SELECT ... INTO FROM ... statement is used to retrieve values from a table and assign them to variables. BigQuery, on the other hand, uses a SET statement to assign values from a subquery to variables.

Syntax

The syntax for the SET statement in BigQuery is as follows:

SET (variable1, variable2, variable3) = (SELECT AS STRUCT column1, column2, column3 FROM table_name WHERE condition LIMIT 1)

Here, we assign the values of column1, column2, and column3 to variable1, variable2, and variable3, respectively, from a table called table_name where a certain condition is met. The LIMIT 1 clause ensures that only one row is returned.

item.title: Google Bigquery Using Sql Udf In Join Predicate With Bigquery
item.description:

Example:

The following code demonstrates an example of using a SQL UDF in a join predicate:

CREATE TEMPORARY FUNCTION game_match(game1 STRING, game2 STRING) AS (
  strpos(game1,game2) >0
);

SELECT 
  t1.gameId 
FROM `bigquery-public-data.baseball.games_post_wide` t1
LEFT JOIN `bigquery-public-data.baseball.games_post_wide` t2 
  ON t1.gameId=t2.gameId AND game_match(t1.gameId, t2.gameId)

The game_match function returns true if the second string is found within the first string and false otherwise. The query selects the gameId from the left table while joining the table on the gameId field and using the game_match function in the join predicate.

item.description:
When working with calculations in BigQuery that involve division, there is a risk of encountering “division by zero” errors. To mitigate this issue, you can use the SAFE_DIVIDE function or the NULLIF function. Let’s explore both methods:

Using SAFE_DIVIDE Function

The SAFE_DIVIDE function provides a safe way to perform division and returns NULL when the divisor is zero. Here’s an example:

ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(SUM(CASE WHEN Name LIKE '%MIKE%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), COUNT(Name) * 100), 1) AS Percentage_of_MIKE

Explanation:

  • The SUM function counts the occurrences of ‘MIKE’ in the Name column.
  • The COUNT function calculates the total number of names.
  • The SAFE_DIVIDE function safely divides the count of ‘MIKE’ by the total count of names, multiplying the result by 100.
  • The ROUND function rounds off the result to one decimal place.

Using NULLIF Function

item.title: Hibernate Oracle Sequence Gap
item.description:
Hibernate Oracle Sequence Gap Explanation of Hibernate Oracle Sequence Producing Large Gap

Summary

In this code, an Oracle sequence is used for generating subject IDs when creating new subjects. The Hibernate framework is used for handling database operations. Although, the sequence produces a large gap in the subject IDs.

Explanation

The table ‘subject’ is created with the following columns: SUBJECT_ID, FNAME, LNAME, EMAILADR, and BIRTHDT. The SUBJECT_ID column is defined as the primary key of the table using the data_index tablespace. A sequence named ‘sub_seq’ is created with a minimum value of 1, maximum value of 999999999999999999999999999, cached in blocks of 100 with no cycle. This sequence is used for generating new subject IDs. The Subject class is defined as an entity using the @Entity and @Table annotations. The @Id annotation specifies that the subjectId field is mapped to the SUBJECT_ID column in the ‘subject’ table. The @GeneratedValue annotation specifies that the subjectId field is generated using a sequence named ‘SUB_SEQ’. The @SequenceGenerator annotation provides additional configuration for the ‘SUB_SEQ’ sequence. When a new subject is added using Hibernate, the sequence number jumps to 255050 resulting in large gaps in the subject IDs. This is because the sequence is cached and values are pulled from the cache in blocks of 100 to improve performance. The cache size can be adjusted to reduce the size of the gaps.

item.title: How To Delete Oracle Schema Contents Quickly
item.description:
How to Delete Oracle Schema Contents Quickly or any other Q&A website without proper attribution and confirmation from the author/owner.

How can I delete all contents in a schema in Oracle?
To delete all contents in a schema in Oracle, you can use the following script:

BEGIN
   FOR cur_rec IN (SELECT object_name, object_type
                   FROM user_objects
                   WHERE object_type IN ('TABLE', 'VIEW', 'PACKAGE', 'SEQUENCE', 'MATERIALIZED VIEW'))
   LOOP
      BEGIN
         EXECUTE IMMEDIATE ('DROP ' || cur_rec.object_type || ' "' || cur_rec.object_name || '" CASCADE CONSTRAINTS');
      EXCEPTION
         WHEN OTHERS THEN
            DBMS_OUTPUT.put_line ('FAILED: DROP ' || cur_rec.object_type || ' "' || cur_rec.object_name || '": ' || SQLERRM);
      END;
   END LOOP;
END;
/

This script will drop all tables, views, packages, sequences, and materialized views in the schema. It also drops their associated constraints.

item.title: How To Get List Of Tables In Google Bigquery Ordered By Size
item.description:
Get List of Google BigQuery Tables Order By Size
When working with Google BigQuery to store and analyze data, foremost to keep track of the size of your tables to optimize performance and minimize storage costs. Luckily, BigQuery offers a simple way to get a list of tables ordered by size using Standard SQL.

The Code:

#standardSQL
SELECT table_id,
    DATE(TIMESTAMP_MILLIS(creation_time)) AS creation_date,
    DATE(TIMESTAMP_MILLIS(last_modified_time)) AS last_modified_date,
    row_count,
    size_bytes,
    CASE
        WHEN type = 1 THEN 'table'
        WHEN type = 2 THEN 'view'
        WHEN type = 3 THEN 'external'
        ELSE '?'
    END AS type,
    TIMESTAMP_MILLIS(creation_time) AS creation_time,
    TIMESTAMP_MILLIS(last_modified_time) AS last_modified_time,
    dataset_id,
    project_id
FROM `yourProject.yourDataset.__TABLES__`
ORDER BY size_bytes DESC

Explanation:

  • The first line specifies the use of Standard SQL by using the #standardSQL directive.
  • The SELECT statement selects the columns or expressions to be retrieved from the tables.
  • table_id identifies the name of the table.
  • creation_date and last_modified_date represent the date when the table was created and last modified respectively, in the format of yyyy-mm-dd.
  • row_count represents the total number of rows in the table.
  • size_bytes represents the total size of the table in bytes.
  • CASE statement maps the integer values of type column to their corresponding string values representing the type of the table, namely: table, view, external; or a question mark if the value is unknown.
  • creation_time and last_modified_time represent the date and time when the table was created and last modified respectively, in UNIX timestamp format.
  • dataset_id and project_id represent the ID of the dataset and project where the table resides.
  • The FROM statement specifies the source tables or views from which to retrieve data. In this case, __TABLES__ represents a system table that lists all tables in the specified dataset.
  • The ORDER BY clause sorts the resulting rows by the specified column or expression, in descending order.

Practical Example:

You can run the above query directly in the BigQuery web UI or API to get a list of tables in a specific dataset ordered by size. This can help you identify tables that are occupying more space and decide whether to optimize them or archive them to reduce storage costs.

If you are working with Oracle database and want to get the actual size of a specific row or have a list of the size of all rows in a table, you can use the following SQL query:

SELECT vsize(col1) + vsize(col2) + vsize(col3) + 
long_raw_length_function(long_col) + DBMS_LOB.GETLENGTH(blob_col) 
FROM table 
WHERE id_col = id_val;

The vsize function returns the size in bytes of a column, while the long_raw_length_function function returns the length of a LONG RAW column. The DBMS_LOB.GETLENGTH function returns the length of a BLOB column. By adding the sizes of all columns, you can obtain the actual size of a row in bytes.

item.title: How To Remove Duplicate Rows Based On Attribute In Google Bigquery Sql
item.description:
Removing Duplicate Rows According to an Attribute in Google BigQuery SQL
In order to remove duplicate rows in a Google BigQuery table, we can use the ROW_NUMBER() analytic function in combination with a subquery. Here’s an example:

SELECT
  *
FROM (
  SELECT
    *,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY transactionid ORDER BY transactionid) rownum
  FROM
    result
)
WHERE
  rownum = 1

First, the inner query selects all columns and rows from the result table, and adds a new column called rownum using ROW_NUMBER(). The PARTITION BY clause tells BigQuery to partition the data by the transactionid column, and the ORDER BY clause sorts the partitions by the same column. This means that for each unique transactionid, rows will be numbered starting from 1.

item.title: Insert Data On Oracle Only If Row Is Absent
item.description:
Insert Data on Oracle Only if Row is Absent How to insert a row in Oracle only if it does not already exist?

One option is to use a MERGE statement that allows you to perform INSERT or UPDATE operations based on a condition.

Example

merge into table1 t1
using (select 'value1' as value1, value2 
       from table2 
       where table2.type="ok") t2
on (t1.col1 = t2.value1)
when not matched then
  insert (t1.col1, t1.col2) 
  values (t2.value1, t2.value2);

In this example, the MERGE statement joins the rows from table1 and table2 based on the equality of their columns (col1 and value1). If a matching row exists in table1, the MERGE statement updates its values with those of the corresponding row in table2, otherwise, it inserts the values from the row in table2 into the table1.

item.title: Invalid Cast Error Oracleconnection Not Recognized As Connection Type
item.description:
Invalid Cast Error: OracleConnection Not Recognized as Connection Type How to cast Connection to OracleConnection in Java?
If you are trying to cast Connection to OracleConnection and receiving a ClassCastException, it is probably because the connection retrieved is a Wrapped Connection. You need to retrieve the underlying connection and then cast it to OracleConnection.

Step-by-step explanation of the code:

Let us go through the code line by line:

@Repository
public class AuditLogDAOImpl implements AuditLogDAO {

    @PersistenceContext(unitName="myUnitName")
    EntityManager em;

    @Resource(name = "dataSource")
    DataSource dataSource;

    public void init() {

        try {
            Connection connection = DataSourceUtils.getConnection(dataSource);
            connection = ((org.jboss.resource.adapter.jdbc.WrappedConnection)connection).getUnderlyingConnection(); //Get the underlying connection from wrapped connection
            OracleConnection oracleConnection = (OracleConnection) connection; //Cast connection to OracleConnection

            String metrics[] = new String[OracleConnection.END_TO_END_STATE_INDEX_MAX];
            metrics[OracleConnection.END_TO_END_CLIENTID_INDEX] = "my_new_username";

            oracleConnection.setEndToEndMetrics(metrics, (short) 0);

            java.util.Properties props = new java.util.Properties();
            props.put("osuser", "newValue");

            oracleConnection.setClientInfo(props);

        } catch (SQLException e) {
            e.printStackTrace();
        }
    }
}

The code retrieves a Connection from the dataSource and then retrieves the underlying connection from a Wrapped Connection. The underlying connection is then cast to OracleConnection.

Code:

SELECT *
FROM  all_snapshots;

SELECT * 
FROM all_mviews;

SELECT * 
FROM dba_mviews;

SELECT * 
FROM all_objects 
WHERE OBJECT_TYPE='MATERIALIZED VIEW';

Explanation:

The first query, SELECT * FROM all_snapshots;, retrieves a list of all snapshots in the database. In Oracle terminology, a snapshot is a synonym for a materialized view. Although, this query only returns views that the user has access to.

The DECODE() function is a handy function in Oracle that returns a value by comparing a given expression with a list of values. If the expression matches any value from the list, then the corresponding result is returned. It takes a minimum of three arguments: the expression to evaluate, the search value, and the result value. Optional pairs of search value and result value can follow. If the expression does not match any value from the list, then the default result value is returned. Although, MySQL does not provide a DECODE() function out of the box. What does it mean that Azure Cosmos DB is multi-model?

Azure Cosmos DB is a single NoSQL data engine that can support multiple data models including documents, key-value, graph, and column-family. The database engine is based on the atom-record-sequence (ARS), which consists of atoms, records, and sequences. The different data models are projected and translated onto the ARS-based data model, and the core data model of Cosmos DB is natively accessible from dynamically-typed programming languages and can be exposed as JSON.

Why do NoSQL databases need indexes?

Although NoSQL databases use various data models, such as key-value, document, column family, and graph, they all share a common need for efficient data retrieval. Write Performance:

Cassandra’s write performance is better than MongoDB’s when dealing with large datasets. This is because Cassandra’s storage engine provides constant-time writes, no matter how big the data set is. On the other hand, MongoDB’s write performance suffers due to two reasons: the b-tree based storage engine and the per-database write lock. Although, foremost to note that MongoDB supports a lock per document, not per database, as previously claimed.

NOSQL: Enforcing Foreign Keys in MongoDB: A Guide In this blog post, we will discuss how to enforce foreign keys in NoSQL databases, specifically MongoDB. We will take an example of a collection of documents and how to reference them to another collection.

Let’s say we have a collection of documents as follows:

{ "_id" : 0 , "owner":0 "name":"Doc1"},{ "_id" : 1 , "owner":1, "name":"Doc1"}, etc

				  On the other hand, we have a collection of owners:  
				  

{ "_id" : 0 , "username":"John"}, { "_id" : 1 , "username":"Sam"}

Now we want to ensure that when we insert a document, it references the user in a correct way. In old-school RDBMS, this can easily be done using a foreign key, but MongoDB doesn’t have foreign keys. To handle this, we can check the correctness of the insertion from the business code, but what if an attacker tampers with the request to the server and puts “owner”: 100, and MongoDB doesn’t throw any exception back? To address this situation, we need to ensure that only the application can insert data that follows our referential integrity rules. MongoDB encourages handling foreign-key relationships on the client-side. Still, they also provide the idea of “Database References” - See this help page. Although, using a DBRef is not recommended. Instead, we can embed the owner’s “documents” inside the owner object itself. This is a one-to-one relationship, and it is better to maintain them as embeddings rather than separate collections. Introduction

When designing a database entity for a set of players, we need to consider having a number of fixed fields and a number of variable fields for skill levels. item.title: Nosql Exploring Hamming Distance Similarity Searches In Databases
item.description: NOSQL: Exploring Hamming Distance and Similarity Searches in Databases Summary: The problem at hand is retrieving records from a database based on the similarity of their 32-bit perceptual hashes. The solution presented involves dividing the hash bit string into smaller chunks and querying for an exact match on these chunks. The returned results are then subjected to a bitwise hamming distance computation to determine the actual similarity between the queried hash and the records in the database. This approach is based on a technique called simhash, and was first described by Moses Charikar in a paper.

item.title: Nosql Optimizing Social Network Schema Design
item.description: NOSQL: Optimizing Social Network Schema Design or any other online forum as a primary source. As a developer working on a proof of concept app for a social network, you may be wondering about how best to design the ‘schema’ for your app. One of the primary concerns may be whether to embed a user’s subscriptions or have a separate ‘subscriptions’ collection and use db references. Let’s explore this in detail. ### Embedding subscriptions vs having a separate collection If you choose to embed a user’s subscriptions, you will need to perform a query to get all of a user’s followers. For example, given the following user: { "username" : "alan", "photo": "123.jpg", "subscriptions" : [ {"username" : "john", "status" : "accepted"}, {"username" : "paul", "status" : "pending"} ] } To find all of alan’s subscribers, you’d have to run something like this: db.users.find({'subscriptions.username' : 'alan'}); Although, MongoDB can place indexes on elements which are arrays, so that will make things a lot faster if you are looking for how many friendships a user has. On the other hand, having a separate ‘subscriptions’ collection and using db references can also be a good way to design your schema. This can help reduce the amount of data stored in a single document, making it easier to manage and scale. It can also help to avoid duplicate data, which can become a problem when storing large amounts of data. Although, it may require more complex queries to fetch data in certain cases. ### Recommendations for displaying a list of subscriptions/subscribers When displaying a list of subscriptions/subscribers, you may encounter problems with n+1 because the subscription document only tells you the username of the target user but not other attributes like the profile photo. One way to solve this issue is to use the $lookup pipeline stage in MongoDB. This stage allows you to perform a join-like operation between documents in different collections, based on a common field. For example, to fetch the profile photos of a user’s subscribers, you can run a query like this: db.users.aggregate([ { $match: { username: 'alan' } }, { $lookup: { from: 'users', localField: 'subscriptions.username', foreignField: 'username', as: 'subscribers' } }, { $unwind: '$subscribers', }, { $project: { 'subscribers.username': 1, 'subscribers.photo': 1 } } ]); This query fetches the user document for ‘alan’, and then performs a lookup against the ‘users’ collection, using the ‘subscriptions.username’ field as the local field, and the ‘username’ field as the foreign field. It then adds the fetched documents to a new field called ‘subscribers’. After that, it unwinds the ‘subscribers’ array so that each subscriber becomes a separate document. Lastly, it uses the $project stage to only include the ‘username’ and ‘photo’ fields of the subscriber documents. ### Recap When designing the ‘schema’ for a social network app, the decision to embed subscriptions or have a separate collection with db references depends largely on the specific requirements and use cases of the app. Both approaches have their pros and cons, and careful consideration should be given to each before making a final decision. When displaying a list of subscriptions/subscribers, the $lookup pipeline stage in MongoDB can be a amazing tool to include additional information from related documents.]]>

item.title: Nosql Pros Cons Of Migrating From Mysql To Cassandra
item.description:
NOSQL: Pros and Cons of Migrating from MySQL to Cassandra

Switching from MySQL to Cassandra - Pros/Cons?

If you are thinking about switching from MySQL to Cassandra, you may be wondering about the pros and cons of making such a move. In this Q&A-style post, we will explore what you need to know to make an informed decision.

What are some of the benefits of using Cassandra over MySQL?

  • Scalability: Cassandra is designed to be highly scalable, making it ideal for managing large amounts of data. It is capable of handling a huge volume of both reads and writes.
  • Automatic replication: Cassandra automatically replicates your data across multiple nodes, providing redundancy and high availability.
  • High performance: Cassandra is specifically built for performance, with its distributed architecture enabling lightning-fast data access and retrieval.
  • NoSQL data model: Cassandra’s NoSQL data model is highly flexible, allowing for dynamic and complex data structures.

What are some of the drawbacks of switching to Cassandra?

  • Learning curve: Unless you are familiar with NoSQL databases, there may be a learning curve when switching to Cassandra.
  • Query language: Cassandra uses a different query language than SQL, so queries will need to be re-written.
  • No ACID compliance: Cassandra does not support ACID compliance like MySQL, so data consistency can be more complex to manage.

What are the key features I need to consider for my data model?

  • Order by: Cassandra’s SliceRange can satisfy this requirement.
  • Group by: Since Cassandra is a NoSQL database, grouping is not a feature supported out-of-the-box as it is in SQL. Although, it is possible to implement a similar functionality through the use of map reduce.
  • Many-to-many relations: Cassandra SuperColumns can do well for one-to-many relationships.
  • Full-text search: Lucandra project provides a full-text engine similar to Sphinx in MySQL.

What size of data and workload can I expect to handle on a medium EC2 instance if I switch to Cassandra?

On a medium EC2 instance, you can expect a significant improvement in reads and writes over MySQL. Cassandra’s distributed architecture and built-in replication make it highly effective for handling large amounts of data and high traffic workloads. That being said, you should always consider your specific workload and data requirements before making the switch.

item.title: Nosql Significance Of Eventual Consistency In Cassandra
item.description:
NOSQL: The Significance of Eventual Consistency in Cassandra Learning Eventual Consistency in Cassandra

Introduction to Eventual Consistency in Cassandra

Cassandra is a popular NoSQL database system known for its scalability and fault-tolerance. One of the core concepts of Cassandra is eventual consistency, which is different from traditional SQL databases that emphasize immediate consistency. In Cassandra, data is distributed and replicated among multiple nodes in a cluster, which means that there may be different versions of the same data on different nodes at the same time. The nodes in a single cluster do not contain identical copies of the same data, instead of making it distributed, which makes immediate consistency impossible. In this Q&A Session, we will explain what eventual consistency means in Cassandra, how it works, and how it affects Cassandra’s performance.

Answer:

The approach depends on the Query Access Pattern (QAP). If you need to retrieve all the list items at once, it’s best to keep each item as a separate record. If you need to retrieve a subset of items or run queries on the list items, it’s best to split the list items into multiple records.

item.description:
NOSQL: Understanding Eventual Consistency: A Simple Explanation

Learning Eventual Consistency in Plain English

Eventual consistency is a popular term used in NoSQL, data grids and other distributed storage systems. It is defined as the state of a distributed system, in which all nodes in the system eventually have the same data, after a certain amount of time, even if there are changes being made to it in the meantime.

In simpler terms, eventual consistency means that updates or changes to data in a distributed system are not instantly propagated to all nodes in the system. Instead, it can take some amount of time for updates to reach all nodes, leading to temporary inconsistencies in the data. Eventually, all nodes will have the same consistent view of the data.

item.title: Oracle A Guide To Time Interval Averaging
item.description:
ORACLE: A Guide to Time Interval Averaging In Oracle 10g, you may want to find the average duration for certain operations. The table includes two timestamp fields: starttime and endtime. The solution is to find averages of the durations given by these timestamps using SQL queries. This Q&A Session will explain, line-by-line, how to average time intervals and provide alternative, more efficient ways to achieve the same result.

Summary To average time intervals in Oracle 10g, a SQL query can be used. The average can be calculated using the formula avg(endtime-starttime). Although, there may be inconsistencies in datatypes, which can be solved by converting the duration into seconds using the extract() function. A more efficient way is to use the formula: (sysdate + (endtime - starttime)*24*60*60 - sysdate) If the endtime and starttime aren’t within a second of each other, then you can cast the timestamps as dates and use date arithmetic for the calculation.

item.title: Oracle Aggregating Boolean Columns A Step By Step Guide
item.description:
ORACLE: Aggregating Boolean Columns: A Step-by-Step Guide Aggregating a Boolean Column Explained
Aggregating a Boolean column means to apply an operation that combines multiple rows into a single value. In this case, we want to combine a set of tuples that contain Boolean values using the OR function, and return the result as a single tuple with aggregated Boolean values.

Approach

The easiest way to do this is to use the MAX() function to determine whether a particular Boolean value is present in the group. Since the Boolean data type can be represented as an integer where 1 = True and 0 = False, we can use the MAX() function to find the highest value in the group, which would correspond to the Boolean value of True. Therefore, if a True value is present in the group, then the MAX() function would return 1, which would indicate that the final aggregated value is True. Otherwise, the MAX() function would return 0, which would indicate that the final aggregated value is False.

Explanation of the Problem

The ROWNUM pseudo-column in Oracle returns the row number of a row that is returned by a query. The problem with using ROWNUM is that it is scoped to the query and is evaluated before any ORDER BY clause is applied. This means that if you filter by ROWNUM, you will get unpredictable results if you are trying to return a specific row based on a specific order of data.

item.title: Oracle Choosing Yesterdays Records A Simple Guide
item.description:
ORACLE: Choosing Yesterday’s Records: A Simple Guide In this blog post, we will discuss how to select records only from yesterday in Oracle using SQL queries. We will break down the code line by line and offer alternative ways to achieve the same result.

Code Explanation The following code selects all the records from the order_header table where the tran_date column is equal to yesterday’s date.

select  *
from    order_header oh
where   tran_date = sysdate-1

The sysdate function returns the current date and time. By subtracting one from it, we get yesterday’s date. Although, this code may not always work as expected because the tran_date column may contain timestamps, making it difficult to compare with a full date. To select records only from yesterday, we need to extract the date portion of the tran_date column and compare it to yesterday’s date. One way to do this is to use the trunc function, which returns the date portion of a datetime value. We can use it to truncate both the tran_date and sysdate-1 values to their respective dates and compare them.

item.title: Oracle Creating A Cte With Defined Values Building Your List
item.description:
ORACLE: Creating a CTE with Defined Values: Building Your List Creating a CTE with Hard-Coded Values in Oracle
If you have a list of known values that you want to use in a CTE (Common Table Expression), you can include them using the UNION ALL syntax in Oracle.

Creating a CTE with Hard-Coded Values

To create a CTE with hard-coded values in Oracle, you can use the following syntax:

WITH cte AS (
  SELECT 101 id FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 102 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 105 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 200 FROM dual
)
SELECT *
FROM cte;

In this example, the WITH statement is used to create a CTE named cte that includes four hard-coded values: 101, 102, 105, and 200. The UNION ALL syntax is used to combine these four values into a single result set.

item.title: Oracle Database Throughput A Quick Explanation
item.description:
ORACLE: Database Throughput: A Quick Explanation What is Database Throughput?
When discussing the performance of a database management system, many technical terms come into play. “Throughput” is one of them. But what does it really mean?

Learning the Definition of Throughput

In network communications, throughput refers to the successful delivery of messages over a communication channel. In database management, throughput defines the number of transactions a system can handle per unit of time. In the context of an OLTP database, or an online transaction processing database, throughput is the number of transactions it can process in a second.

item.title: Oracle Date Time Addition Standards What Are They
item.description: ORACLE: Date/Time Addition Standards: What Are They? Standards for adding dates and times can differ across different programming languages and tools. One common concern is what happens when adding a month to a date - should the result be the last day of the next month, the first day of the month after that, or something else entirely? While there is no universal standard for this, some programming languages and organizations have outlined their own guidelines. For example, the POSIX.1-2001 standard suggests adjusting the values until they fit, which can result in different dates depending on the month and year. Meanwhile, SQL-92 considers asking for the next month from January 31 to be an error. Ultimately, the choice of how to handle date and time addition can depend on the specific requirements of the project or domain. It’s essential to carefully consider how different options could impact the functionality and usability of the application.

item.description:
ORACLE: Demystifying Database Pagination: An Explanation of How it Works How does pagination of results in databases work?
Pagination of results in databases is a technique that helps to retrieve a subset of data from a database table, in a series of chunks or pages. This approach is often used in web applications where data needs to be displayed to users in a user-friendly format. Instead of retrieving all data at once, pagination queries a subset of data, allowing for quick and efficient data retrieval. This data retrieval technique applies to various databases such as MySQL, Oracle DB, and others.

item.title: Oracle Detecting Cycles Through Recursive Subquery Factoring
item.description: ORACLE: Detecting Cycles through Recursive Subquery Factoring Cycle detection is a crucial task in database systems to avoid infinite loops when querying hierarchical data. Oracle SQL has provided hierarchical queries using CONNECT BY syntax since version 2. In their latest Oracle 11g release 2, they introduced recursive subquery factoring, also known as the recursive with clause. This clause follows the ANSI standard and has been implemented in several RDBMS vendors.

item.title: Oracle Difference Between Database Tablespace
item.description: ORACLE: The Difference Between Database and Tablespace Summary: In Oracle, a database is defined as the set of files that contain all the data while an instance includes the processes and memory areas that enable Oracle database to function. Tablespaces, on the other hand, are logical storage units within the database that usually consist of one or more data files. They allow you to separate different applications on the same database system for better storage and handling purposes.

Difference between <> and != in SQL

In SQL, both <> and != are used to represent Not Equal To operations. They both serve the same purpose, but <> is ISO standard, while != is not.

Let’s take an example to know both operators:

SELECT * FROM students WHERE roll_no != 2;

The above query will return all the records from the students table except the record with roll_no = 2.

item.title: Oracle Eliminating Subtype Dependency A Guide
item.description:
ORACLE: Eliminating Subtype Dependency: A Guide Eliminating Subtype Dependency in Oracle

Introduction

In Oracle, subtypes are a way to create new types from existing ones, with additional constraints. Although, this can sometimes result in a lot of redundant code, especially if you need to write the same functions and procedures for different subtypes. In this blog post, we will explore some ways to eliminate subtype dependency in Oracle.

The Problem

Let’s consider the following example. We have a package called “so1” that defines two subtypes - “foo_t” and “bar_t”. We also have two associated types - “foolist” and “barlist”, which are table types of “foo_t” and “bar_t” respectively. We then have two procedures called “set”, one for each subtype, which takes an ID and a list of values as input, and inserts them into a table called “so1table”. Lastly, we have two functions called “to_str”, again one for each subtype, which converts a list of values into a string.

item.title: Oracle Fetch Vs For Choosing Right Looping Method For Cursor In Pl Sql
item.description:
ORACLE: FETCH vs FOR: Choosing the Right Looping method for Cursor in PL/SQL Learning the difference between FETCH/FOR to loop a CURSOR in PL/SQL
PL/SQL offers two ways to loop through a cursor, which allows you to execute the same SELECT statement multiple times with different values. The first method involves using the OPEN-FETCH-CLOSE syntax, while the second method utilizes a FOR loop.

What are the differences between FETCH and FOR loops?

FETCH loops require explicit cursor declarations and give access to variables such as %ROWCOUNT, %ROWTYPE, %FOUND, %NOTFOUND, and %ISOPEN. On the other hand, FOR loops do not require explicit cursor declarations but do not give access to these variables.

When trying to create a user or role with an invalid name, Oracle throws an ORA-65096 error. This error indicates that the user or role name you’re trying to create is not valid for common users or roles. Common user and role names must start with C## or c## and consist only of ASCII characters.

item.title: Oracle How To Check If A Database Table Contains Data With Sql Code
item.description:
ORACLE: How to Check if a Database Table Contains Data with SQL Code In this question, the user wants to check a condition based on the count of a column from a table. If the count is greater than zero, they want to update the same table, otherwise, they do not want to update it.

The initial code provided is as follows:

if (select count(column) from table) > 0 then   if (condition) > 0 then     update table   else      do not update   end if; end if; ```  Here, if the count of the column is greater than zero, the inner if condition is evaluated. If it is greater than zero, the table is updated, and if it is not, the table is not updated. Although, this code might not work in certain databases like Oracle.  Therefore, a better way to write this code would be:  ``` declare   value\_count number; begin   select count(column) into value\_count from table;      if value\_count > 0 then     if (condition) > 0 then       update table     else       -- do not update     end if;   end if; end; ```  Here, we first declare a variable `value\_count` of `number` datatype. We then use the `select` statement to count the number of rows in the table and store the result in the `value\_count` variable using the `into` keyword.  After that, we check if the `value\_count` is greater than zero. If it is, we evaluate the inner `if` condition. If the condition is true, we update the table, otherwise, we do not update it.  It is to be noted that the code within the `else` block of the inner `if` condition is not required as it does nothing when executed. It can be removed to reduce the complexity of the code.  An alternative way to accomplish the same task would be to use a single SQL statement:  ``` update table set column = new\_value where (select count(column) from table) > 0 and (condition) > 0; ```  Here, we use the `update` statement to update the table `set`ting the value of `column` to the `new\_value`, but only if the count of rows in the table is greater than zero and the `condition` is true.  To summarize, we can use either PL/SQL or SQL statements to achieve the goal of updating a table based on a count of rows from another table. In PL/SQL, we can declare a variable, use the `select` statement to count rows, and then evaluate the conditions using `if` statements. In SQL, we can use the `update` statement with appropriate `where` clauses to accomplish the task.]]>

item.title: Oracle How To Delete All Data From Every Sql Table
item.description:
ORACLE: How to Delete All Data from Every SQL Table? How to Delete All Data from All Tables in Oracle DB

If you are maintaining more than 30 tables in Oracle DB and want to delete all the data from these tables without dropping the tables, you can use the following SQL code:

BEGIN
  FOR c IN (SELECT table_name, constraint_name FROM user_constraints WHERE constraint_type='R')
  LOOP
    EXECUTE IMMEDIATE ('alter table ' || c.table_name || ' disable constraint ' || c.constraint_name);
  END LOOP;
  FOR c IN (SELECT table_name FROM user_tables)
  LOOP
    EXECUTE IMMEDIATE ('truncate table ' || c.table_name);
  END LOOP;
  FOR c IN (SELECT table_name, constraint_name FROM user_constraints WHERE constraint_type='R')
  LOOP
    EXECUTE IMMEDIATE ('alter table ' || c.table_name || ' enable constraint ' || c.constraint_name);
  END LOOP;
END;

This code first disables all referential integrity constraints for all tables. It then truncates all the tables to delete all data. Lastly, it enables all the referential integrity constraints for all tables.

item.description:
ORACLE: JDBC Default AutoCommit Behavior: A Quick Overview Learning Default AutoCommit Behavior in JDBC Connection to Oracle
When working with JDBC to connect to an Oracle database, there are certain default behaviors that need to be understood. Specifically, the autoCommit behavior of the JDBC connection is an important aspect to take into account when working with transactions.

What is AutoCommit Behavior?

AutoCommit behavior determines whether or not every individual SQL statement is automatically committed right after it is executed. When a connection is created, it is in AutoCommit mode by default. This means that every SQL statement is treated as a transaction, and it is automatically committed right after it is executed. Although, the default behavior is for a SQL statement to be committed when it is completed, not when it is executed. A statement is considered completed when all of its result sets and update counts have been retrieved. In almost all cases, a statement is completed, and therefore committed, right after it is executed, but foremost to keep this behavior in mind when working with JDBC.

public class oraDbContext : DbContext
{
    static oraDbContext() {
        Database.SetInitializer(null);     }      public oraDbContext(string connName)         : base("Name=" + connName) { }      public \_schema1 schema1 = \_schema1.Instance;     public \_schema2 schema2 = \_schema2.Instance;      protected override void OnModelCreating(DbModelBuilder modelBuilder) {         schema1.OnModelCreating(modelBuilder);         schema2.OnModelCreating(modelBuilder);     } } ```  This class extends the DbContext class provided by Entity Framework and sets up the necessary database information. The static constructor sets the database initializer to null to prevent database initialization from occurring. The constructor takes a connection string name as an argument and passes it to the base constructor. Two public fields are created for each schema, schema1 and schema2, which are instances of their corresponding schema classes (_schema1 and _schema2). Lastly, the OnModelCreating method is overridden to set up the schema configurations using their corresponding methods.  Next, let's take a look at the _schema1 class:  ``` public sealed class \_schema1 {     private static readonly \_schema1 instance = new \_schema1();      static \_schema1() { }     private \_schema1() { }      public static \_schema1 Instance {         get {             return instance;         }     }      public DbSet someTable { get; set; }

    internal void OnModelCreating(DbModelBuilder modelBuilder) {
        modelBuilder.Configurations.Add(new someTableMap());
    }
}

This class uses the singleton pattern to ensure that only one instance of the class is created. It contains a public property for the table and an internal method to set up the table configuration. In this case, it adds the configuration for the someTable table using the someTableMap class.

item.title: Oracle Mechanics Of Pl Sqls Contains Function Explained
item.description:
ORACLE: The Mechanics of PL-SQL’s contains() Function Explained Summary:

The PL-SQL contains() method is used on text fields that have a ‘CONTEXT Index’ to search for specific strings. It counts how many times a string occurs in a text field and returns the rows where the string exists.

The standard usage of contains() is as follows:

SELECT score(1), value FROM table_name WHERE CONTAINS(textField, ‘searchString’, 1) > 0; Explanation: The above query is used to find rows where the string ‘searchString’ exists in the textField of the table. The ‘score’ operator is used to display the results based on the number of times the string is found in the text field. For example, if we have a table named ’table_name’ with three columns - value, textField, and id - and the following data: value | textField |— 2 | A 1 | C Explanation of the code example: The code example from Oracle’s documentation is used to display the top 10 news Q&A Sessions that contain the word ‘oracle’. The code starts by declaring a variable named ‘rowno’ and initializing it to 0. It then uses a ‘for loop’ to iterate through the results of the query. The query selects the score and title from the ’news’ table where the ’text’ column contains the word ‘oracle’. The loop increases the ‘rowno’ variable by 1 for each iteration and outputs the title and score of the current row using the ‘dbms_output.put_line’ function. The code exits the loop after outputting the top 10 rows using the ’exit when rowno = 10;’ statement. Rewritten code: DECLARE rowno NUMBER := 0; BEGIN FOR c1 IN ( SELECT SCORE(1) score, title FROM news WHERE CONTAINS(text, ‘oracle’, 1) > 0 ORDER BY SCORE(1) DESC ) LOOP rowno := rowno + 1; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(c1.title||’: ‘||c1.score); EXIT WHEN rowno = 10; END LOOP; END; Practical examples: The contains() method can be used in many practical scenarios, such as searching for specific words in text fields or finding relevant documents. For example, a company may use contains() to search for resumes that match specific keywords when hiring new employees. Another practical use case is searching for relevant documents in legal cases by using keywords. Alternative ways: If you cannot use contains(), you can use the ’like’ operator to search for specific strings in text fields. Although, like does not provide the same level of accuracy and speed as contains() since it does not use a CONTEXT Index. Another alternative is using regular expressions to search for specific patterns in text fields. Regular expressions can be amazing, but they can also be complex and may not be as efficient as contains() for large datasets. References: - Oracle: https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/ccapp/overview-text-query-language.html - DBA Oracle: http://www.dba-oracle.com/t _sql_contains_clause.htm]]>

item.description:
ORACLE: Optimizing CLOB Performance with SUBSTR Function or any other forum as a reference, only use reputable sources.)

In a PL/SQL procedure, SUBSTR is used extensively on a VARCHAR2 parameter. To remove the length limit, the parameter was changed to a CLOB, but performance was observed to suffer. This prompted a series of tests to determine the cause of the decreased performance, based on previous experiments from 2005. The test results show that SUBSTR(VARCHAR2) is the fastest, followed by DBMS_LOB.SUBSTR, and then CLOB SUBSTR. This contradicts previous test results and prompts the question of why this is happening. To further investigate, the test was expanded by increasing the string length to 30 characters and performing 10 test runs. The results showed VARCHAR2 SUBSTR performed fastest, while CLOB SUBSTR had the worst performance. Although, DBMS_LOB.SUBSTR performed similarly to VARCHAR2 SUBSTR. Changing the substring range to 5,14 (14,5 for DBMS_LOB.SUBSTR), and then to 17,14 (14,17 for DBMS_LOB.SUBSTR), resulted in DBMS_LOB.SUBSTR still performing similarly to VARCHAR2 SUBSTR, while CLOB SUBSTR performance continued to lag behind. It is important to note that the specific hardware and Oracle versions used in the experiment may have an impact on performance. Although, the results suggest that DBMS_LOB.SUBSTR may be a viable alternative when needing to perform SUBSTR on CLOB data types. Overall, foremost to consider performance factors when working with large text data in PL/SQL procedures, and to choose the appropriate data type and method to optimize performance.]]>
